question: what linguistics features are used?

evidence: Table TABREF17 lists the features that we used for CE recovery. We used Farasa to perform segmentation and POS tagging and to determine stem-templates BIBREF31. Farasa has a reported POS accuracy of 96% on the WikiNews dataset BIBREF31. Though the Farasa diacritizer utilizes a combination of some the features presented herein, namely segmentation, POS tagging, and stem templates, Farasa's SVM-ranking approach requires explicit specification of feature combinations (ex. $Prob(CE\Vert current\_word, prev\_word, prev\_CE)$). Manual exploration of the feature space is undesirable, and ideally we would want our learning algorithm to do so automatically. The flexibility of the DNN model allowed us to include many more surface level features such as affixes, leading and trailing characters in words and stems, and the presence of words in large gazetteers of named entities. As we show later, these additional features significantly lowered CEER.

title: Arabic Diacritic Recovery Using a Feature-Rich biLSTM Model
answer_short: surface-level features, morphological features, syntactic features, POS tags, gender and number features, affixes, leading and trailing characters, named entities, and case endings
answer_rationale: The document explicitly lists multiple linguistic features used in the diacritization models, including surface-level features (e.g., word surface forms, affixes), morphological features (e.g., stem templates, morphological patterns), syntactic features (e.g., POS tags, gender and number), and contextual features (e.g., leading/trailing characters, named entities). These are detailed in sections discussing feature types for both core-word and case-ending diacritization, such as Text 18, Text 26, and Text 65.
